 Darryn Peterson leads Utah Jazz in Loss to Timberwolves: Key Takeaways 
 Eric Spyropoulos ● @EricSpyroNBA Digital Writer November 8, 2026 8:16 PM MST The shorthanded Utah Jazz continue to fight.
 On the final stop of their four-game road trip, the Jazz went to battle against a surging Minnesota Timberwolves squad without Lauri Markkanen, who missed Sunday’s game as a result of the right wrist sprain suffered just under two weeks ago. 
 The Jazz had pockets of stingy defense Sunday night, while their backcourt duo of Darryn Peterson (26 points, four assists) and Keyonte George (19 points, eight assists) joined forces to lead the offense. Unfortunately, Utah couldn’t avoid putting the Timberwolves on the line (27-of-32) and weren’t consistently able to knock down shots (42.5 percent from the field and 29.2 percent from deep) in a 115-100 loss. 
 “Another game where there’s tons of positives but we don’t get the result to show for it,” said Jazz head coach Will Hardy. “I thought the team’s process offensively was pretty good… We’re just struggling to get over the hump right now.” 
 Although it was a slow start to the game offensively for the Jazz, they went back-and-forth with Minnesota as a result of stingy defense. Minnesota only shot 41 percent from the field during the opening quarter, with most of the damage done in the paint (16 points). Meanwhile, Utah’s scoring was a balanced distribution both in terms of shot location (three 3-pointers and 10 points in the paint) and responsibility (five Jazzmen scored five points in the frame). Minnesota got 16 points off the bench, which helped push the home team to a slight 28-25 lead after 12 minutes.
 Neither team gained separation as the second quarter got underway, as both squads continued to search for a rhythm. Utah’s second unit continued to struggle during this stretch, as the visitors couldn’t generate clean looks on the offensive end on a consistent basis. As a result, the Timberwolves opened their first double-digit lead of the game, which reached 10 near the midway point of the frame. Keyonte George (11 points, seven assists) and Darryn Peterson (12 points, three assists) joined forces to keep Utah within striking distance, but Minnesota still took a 57-51 advantage into the halftime break.
 The Jazz raced out of the gates with back-to-back 3-pointers to tie the game at 57, which then transitioned to a back-and-forth affair in the ensuing minutes. Minnesota used a 7-0 spurt midway through the third quarter to regain control, as a few untimely turnovers stagnated Utah’s offense. The Timberwolves were able to get to the free-throw line often during the frame (11-of-12), which helped generate enough offense to pull away with a 90-78 lead heading into the final quarter. 
 Utah’s offense went cold to start the fourth frame, as the visitors couldn’t generate a point through the first three minutes. To make matters worse, George rolled his ankle while running up the floor after a Timberwolves basket and had to exit the game. Peterson attempted to lead a Jazz comeback, but Utah could only get within 10 points down the stretch as Minnesota countered with timely shots to keep the visitors at bay. 
 Here are three takeaways from Sunday’s action. 
 Utah’s backcourt led the way  
 The on-court chemistry of George and Peterson has continued to be a work in progress for the Jazz early in the season. 
 Both players possess the ability to score from all three levels and handle the ball, with the combination proving to be very effective Sunday night in Minneapolis. In the first half, George thrived as a playmaker (seven assists) as he continued to rely on inside scoring to fuel an 11-point half. Meanwhile, Peterson chipped in with 12 points and three assists on 5-of-10 shooting from the field, mixing up his scoring between deep shots (two threes) and floaters in the paint.
 Throughout the second half, both players continued to impact the game and lead Utah’s offense. The guard duo combined for 16 points in the third frame before Peterson had to shoulder the load in the fourth after George’s injury. 
 In the end, George exited early with 19 points and eight assists, while Peterson finished with 26 points, six rebounds, and four assists. The rookie guard knocked down four threes (a career-high) and finished plus-3 in the box score. 
 “I thought Darryn turned in his best game as a pro,” Hardy said. “There’s a variety of ways to attack. There’s a lot to take away from how he not only handled ball pressure, but also an elite big at the rim.” 
 Utah competed defensively  
 One of the main reasons Utah was able to remain within striking distance for much of Sunday’s game was the team’s effort on the defensive end. 
 The Jazz weren’t particularly efficient during the first half (45 percent from the field with seven turnovers), but the visitors continued to fight on the other end of the floor and limited Minnesota to an identical 45-percent effort with seven turnovers across the first two quarters. 
 Utah was active in the passing lanes, with five steals helping to fuel a productive half in transition (16 points). 
 In the third quarter, the Jazz were active defensively (six forced turnovers) but struggled to defend without fouling, which helped Minnesota generate offense. By the final buzzer, the Timberwolves had coughed it up 22 times, but had enough success inside the paint (50 points) and from the stripe (27 points) to lead to a home win. It also helped Minnesota’s cause that the home team went 6-of-12 from beyond the arc during the second half. 
 “They got away from us at the free-throw line,” Hardy said.”We didn’t do a great job of keeping our body positioning in front, and they played through our hip and put us in positions where we had to foul.”
 In the loss, Utah finished with 10 steals as a team, with Ace Bailey leading the team’s efforts in that area (four steals). 
 Minnesota’s bench thrived  
 With Markkanen joining Jaren Jackson Jr. and Jusuf Nurkić on the sidelines, Utah’s shorthanded rotation faced another challenge. 
 Hardy turned to Kyle Filipowski off the bench, with the third-year big man contributing nine points and five rebounds in his 13 minutes on the floor during Sunday’s loss. 
 “He gave us some physicality in the interior and it was nice to see him hit the catch-and-shoot three,” Hardy said of Filipowski. “He’s a very skilled player, a good ball mover, and screener. I thought Kyle played like Kyle.” 
 However, the Jazz second unit struggled to find a flow throughout the night, which stood out in comparison to the success generated by Minnesota’s bench.
 Led by Bones Hyland (14 points), the Timberwolves’ second unit scored 35 points, with all five players finishing plus-11 or higher in the box score. Utah got just 20 points off its bench, with Hardy going six deep on the second unit in hopes of finding a spark. 
 The Jazz return home to host the Miami Heat on Tuesday (7 p.m. MT, Jazz+).
